title: Can Latin America Become a Data Center Powerhouse?
gist: Latin American governments in Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and Chile are racing to attract AI data centers, helped by US local opposition to the facilities and by tax incentives, and the region already hosts more than 500 data centers. Andrés Oppenheimer argues that political risk, weak grids and shrinking hardware footprints temper the opportunity, and that data centers create few jobs unless paired with education reform and AI adoption by small businesses.

themes.theme: US data center backlash pushes capex abroad

insights.claim: A Gallup poll published in 2026 found that 71% of Americans oppose construction of a data center near them, and growing local resistance is leading Big Tech companies to look abroad for sites.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Permitting friction in the US could redirect hyperscaler data center capex toward Latin America and other regions.
insights.quote: A Gallup poll published this year found that 71% of Americans oppose nearby data center construction.
insights.locator: Milei argued that Argentina has abundant energy

insights.claim: According to the article, global demand for data is growing about 20% a year, and the Inter-American Development Bank reported that Latin America is already experiencing a significant boom in data center investment.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Structural data demand growth supports long-run demand for digital infrastructure assets in the region.
insights.quote: Latin America is already experiencing “a significant boom in data center investment.”

themes.theme: Regional race for data center investment

insights.claim: Argentine President Javier Milei argues Argentina can become a regional or global data center hub thanks to abundant energy, rare earth minerals, human capital, vast territory and cold climates that make cooling cheaper.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Argentina is positioning data centers as a pillar of its growth strategy, which matters for energy and infrastructure plays there.
insights.quote: “Data centers will generate a phenomenal acceleration of economic growth”

insights.claim: Milei has submitted a bill for a new AI legal framework that includes a commitment to keep AI unregulated and creates a new business category, the 'non-human corporation', for companies operated by AI agents.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: A deliberately light-touch AI regime could make Argentina a regulatory-arbitrage destination for AI firms.
insights.locator: A few months after our interview

insights.claim: Brazilian President Lula signed an executive order exempting data centers from federal import taxes on servers and refrigeration parts, which Brazil's Finance Ministry says could draw $377 billion in investment over the next decade.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Tax incentives make Brazil a leading candidate for regional hyperscale buildouts, benefiting equipment, power and real estate providers.
insights.quote: this framework could draw $377 billion in new investments over the next decade

insights.claim: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum celebrated a $4.8 billion investment in six data centers in Querétaro, and the Mexican Data Center Association forecasts $82.5 billion of sector investment between 2026 and 2031.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Querétaro is emerging as a nearshore data center cluster positioned as a gateway between the US and Latin America.

insights.claim: Rodrigo Durán of the Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index says northern Chile already has an energy surplus that is being thrown away, plus direct submarine fiber-optic cables to the United States, making it attractive for data centers.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Curtailed renewable power in northern Chile could be monetized through data center demand.
insights.quote: “Chile’s northern region already has an energy surplus that is literally being thrown away.

insights.claim: Latin America already hosts more than 500 data centers, including hyperscale facilities used by Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Google.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: An existing hyperscaler footprint lowers the barrier to further expansion in the region.
insights.locator: Despite these hurdles, most industry experts

insights.claim: OpenAI and Argentina's Sur Energy signed a letter of intent in October 2025 to explore a $25 billion Stargate data center project in Argentina, but construction is not known to have started.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Headline mega-projects in the region can stall at the letter-of-intent stage, so announced capex should be discounted.
insights.quote: to “bring the first Stargate project to Latin America.” But so far, construction is not known to have started

themes.theme: Risks to the Latin data center thesis

insights.claim: According to a UN study, Latin America and the Caribbean received only about 1.6% of the world's spending on artificial intelligence in 2023, partly because of political and economic uncertainty.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: The region's small share of AI spending shows how far the hype is from actual capital flows.
insights.quote: Latin America and the Caribbean received only about 1.6% of the world’s spending on artificial intelligence
insights.locator: In 2023, Latin America and the Caribbean

insights.claim: Billion-dollar data center investments in Latin America face the risk that governments change the rules, including nationalization, and that local power grids are unreliable.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Grid reliability and rule-of-law risk may cap hyperscaler commitments, making power infrastructure a prerequisite investment.
insights.quote: can they rely on local power grids?
insights.locator: And even if investors receive written guarantees

insights.claim: If new technologies shrink servers and make cooling more efficient, Latin America's touted advantages of huge territory, abundant energy and proximity could lose their pull for data center location.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains in compute are a technological risk to long-dated land and power-based data center theses.
insights.quote: If future data centers require much smaller, less energy-hungry facilities, the allure of building them south of the border may quickly disappear.

insights.claim: Economist Eduardo Levy Yeyati likens data centers to an extractive industry like mining that can be profitable and generate tax revenue but does little for employment.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Data center booms may not ease social or employment pressures, limiting their political payoff for host governments.
insights.quote: “It’s an extractive industry, much like mining. It can be profitable and bring in tax dollars, but it won’t do much for employment,”

themes.theme: Education and SME AI adoption gap

insights.claim: According to the UN, only 22% of adults over 25 in Brazil and Mexico have tertiary education, compared with nearly 60% in Japan and 55% in South Korea, and the region lags far behind Asia on PISA scores.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Human capital gaps limit Latin America's ability to move up the AI value chain beyond hosting infrastructure.
insights.quote: only 22% of adults over 25 in Brazil and Mexico have tertiary education, compared to nearly 60% in Japan and 55% in South Korea

insights.claim: The author predicts Latin America will lose millions of jobs to automation, perhaps more than other regions, as manufacturing and services like call centers are replaced by algorithms, and risks permanent dependence on foreign tech giants unless it builds its own AI models such as Latam-GPT and Sabiá.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: AI-driven job losses in BPO and manufacturing could add social and political instability in the region.

insights.claim: Small and medium-sized enterprises account for more than 95% of Latin America's companies and employ 60% of its formal workforce, according to a UN report.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Productivity gains from AI in the region depend on adoption by SMEs, not on infrastructure alone.
insights.quote: These businesses account for more than 95% of the region’s companies and employ 60% of its formal workforce

insights.claim: Columbia University professor Raul Katz argues the biggest barrier to AI in Latin America is not infrastructure but adoption by SMEs, and calls for regional technology institutes modeled on Germany's Fraunhofer institutes.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Spending on AI enablement and training for SMEs may unlock more value than data center buildouts.
insights.quote: “While you certainly need data centers in Latin America, the biggest barrier isn’t infrastructure—it’s AI adoption by small and medium-sized enterprises,”

insights.claim: The author criticizes right-of-center Latin American leaders for copying Donald Trump's playbook of slashing public university and research budgets, arguing this undermines the region's ability to build modern AI-era economies.
insights.speaker: ANDRÉS OPPENHEIMER
insights.so_what: Pro-market fiscal austerity may come at the expense of long-run productivity and competitiveness in technology.
insights.quote: starving education, science and technology cannot build modern economies
